readings.head: {{RunningHeader|wilful|6926|will}}

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wilful|6926|will}}</noinclude>mands, or instructions; obstinate; stubborn; refractory; wayward; inflexible: as, a ''wilful'' man; a ''wilful'' horse.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like a ''wilful'' youth,
That which I owe is lost.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 1. 146.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''wilfu''’ man never wanted woe.
{{right|''Battle of Pentland Hills'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 242).}}</poem>}}

'''Wilful fire-raising.''' Same as ''arson''<sup>1</sup>.   [Scotch.]='''Syn. 3.''' ''Untoward, Contrary'', etc. (see ''wayward''), self-willed, mulish, intractable, headstrong, unruly, heady.

'''wilfulhead†''' (wil′fu̇l-hed), ''n.''   [ME. ''wilfulhed''; < ''wilful'' + ''-head''.]   Wilfulness; perverse obstinacy.
{{smaller block|<poem>And nat be lyk tiraunts of Lumbardye,
That usen ''wilfulhed'' and tirannye.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women (1st version), l. 355.}}</poem>}}

'''wilfulling†''', ''n.''   [< ''wilful'' + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.]   A wilful act. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Great King, no more bay with thy ''wilfullings''
His wrath’s dread Torrent.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Lawe.}}</poem>}}

'''wilfully, willfully''' (wil′fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wilfully, wilfulli, wylfully, wilfulliche''; < ''wilful'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Of free will or choice; willingly; voluntarily; gladly; readily.
{{smaller block|Fede ye the flok of God that is among you, and purvey ye, not as constreyned, but ''wilfulli.''
{{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Pet. v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Be nouȝte abasshed to bydde and to be nedy;
Syth he that wrouȝte al the worlde was ''wilfullich'' nedy.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xx. 48.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Trowe ye that whyles I may preche,
And winne gold and silver for I teche,
That I wol lyve in povert ''wilfully''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Pardoner’s Tale, l. 155.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They ''wilfully'' themselves exile from light.</poem> {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 386.}}}}

'''2.''' By design; with set purpose; intentionally; especially, in a wilful manner; as following one’s own will; selfishly; perversely; obstinately; stubbornly.
{{smaller block|<poem>For he that winketh whan he sholde see,
Al ''wilfully'', God lat him never thee.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 612.}}}}
{{smaller block|The mother, . . . being determinately, lest I should say of a great lady ''wilfully'', bent to marry her to Demagoras, tried all ways. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|Surely of such desperat persons as will ''willfully'' followe the course of theyr owne follye there is noe compassion to be had. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}
{{smaller block|If we sin ''wilfully'' after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins. {{right|Heb. x. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|Religion is a matter of our freest choice; and if men will obstinately and ''wilfully'' set themselves against it, there is no remedy. {{right|''Tillotson.''}}}}
'''3.''' In ''law'', ''wilfully'' is sometimes interpreted to mean—(''a'') by an act or an omission done of purpose, with intent to bring about a certain result; or (''b'') with implication of evil intent or legal malice, or with absence of reasonable ground for believing the act in question to be lawful.

'''wilfulness, willfulness''' (wil′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wilfulnesse''; < ''wilful'' + ''-ness''.]   '''1.''' The character of being wilful; determination to have one’s own way; self-will; obstinacy; stubbornness; perverseness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Falshede is soo ful of cursidnesse
that her worship shalle neuere haue enterprise
where it Reigneth and hathe the ''wilfulnesse''.</poem> {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 71.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men of business, absorbed in their object, which calls out daring, energy, resolution, and force, acquire often a ''wilfulness'' of temper. {{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, p. 292.}}}}
'''2.''' Intention; the character of being done by design.
{{smaller block|The deliberateness and ''wilfulness'', or as we prefer to call it the intention, which constitutes the crime of murder.
{{right|''Mozley and Whitely.''}}}}

'''wilily''' (wī′li-li), ''adv.''   [< ''wily'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a wily manner; by stratagem; insidiously; craftily.
{{smaller block|They did work ''wilily''. {{right|Josh. ix. 4.}}}}

'''wiliness''' (wī′li-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being wily; cunning; guile.

'''wilk''' (wilk), ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''whelk.''

'''will'''<sup>1</sup> (wil), ''v.'' Pres. 1 ''will'', 2 ''wilt'', 3 ''will'', pl. ''will''; imperf. 1 ''would'', 2 ''wouldest'' or ''wouldst'', 3 ''would'', pl. ''would'' (obs. pp. ''would'', ''wold''). ''Will''<sup>1</sup> has no imperative and no infinitive. [< ME. ''willen'' (pres. ind. 1st and 3d pers. ''wille'', ''wile'', ''wulle'', ''wule'', ''wolle'', ''wole'', ''wol'', ''woll'' (also contr. ''ulle''); 2d pers. ''wilt'', ''wult'', ''wolt''; pl. ''willeth'', ''wulleth'', ''wolleth''; pret. 1st and 3d pers. ''wolde'' (> E. ''would''), ''wulde'', ''walde'', ''wald'' (> Sc. ''wad''), 2d pers. ''woldest'', ''woldes'', pl. ''wolden'', ''wolde'', ''wulde'', ''walde'', pp. ''wold''; < AS. ''willan'', ''wyllan'' (pres. ind. 1st and 3d pers. ''wile'', ''wyle'', ''wille'', ''wylle'', 2d pers. ''wilt'', pl. ''willath'', ''wyllath'', pret. 1st and 3d pers. ''wolde'', 2d pers. ''woldest'', pl. ''woldon'', ppr. ''willende'') = OS. ''willian'', ''wellian'' = OFries. ''willa'', ''wella'' = D. ''willen'' = MLG. LG. ''willen'' = OHG. ''wellan'', ''wollan'', MHG. ''wellen'', ''wollen'', G. ''wollen'' = Icel. ''vilja'' = Sw. ''vilja'' = Dan. ''ville'' = Goth. ''wiljan'' (pret. ''wilda'') = OBulg. ''voliti'', will, ''velieti'', command, = Russ. ''velieti'', command, etc., = Lith. ''woliti'', will, = L. ''velle'' (pres. ind. ''volo''), wish. Prob. not connected, as usually asserted, with Gr. βούλεσθαι, will, wish, or with Skt. ''var'', choose, select, prefer. From the same source are ult. E. ''will''<sup>2</sup>, ''wale''<sup>2</sup>, ''wiln'', ''well''<sup>2</sup>, ''weal''<sup>1</sup>, ''wild''<sup>1</sup>, ''wilful'', etc. From the L. verb are ult. E. ''volition'', ''voluntary'', ''volunteer'', ''volunty'', ''voluptuary'', etc., ''nolens volens'', etc.] '''A.''' As an independent verb. '''I.''' ''trans.'' To wish; desire; want; be willing to have (a certain thing done): now chiefly used in the subjunctive (optative) preterit form ''would'' governing a clause: as, I ''would'' that the day were at hand. When in the first person the subject is frequently omitted: as, ''would'' that ye had listened to us!
{{smaller block|''Wol'' sche ȝit my sone hire wedde & to wife haue?
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4203.}}}}
{{smaller block|“The toure vp the toft,” quod she, “treuthe is there-inne, And ''wolde'' that ȝe wrouȝte as his worde techeth.”
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), i. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|I ''wol'' him noght thogh thou were deed tomorwe.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 307.}}}}
{{smaller block|And when thei were come to Merlyn, he thanked hem of that thei hadde seide, and that ''wolde'' hym so moche gode.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|Here I ''would'' not More to flit from his literal plain sense.
{{right|''Tyndale'', Ans. to Sir T. More (Parker Soc.), p. 252.}}}}
{{smaller block|She moved him to ask of her father a field; and she lighted from off her ass; and Caleb said unto her: What ''wilt'' thou?
{{right|Judges i. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Is this thy vengeance, holy Venus, thine,
Because I ''would'' not one of thine own doves,
Not ev’n a rose, were offer’d to thee?</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lucretius.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Would'' in optative expressions is often followed by a dative, with or without ''to'', noting the person or power by whom the wish may be fulfilled: hence the phrases ''would'' (''to'')
{{right|''God'', ''would'' (''to'') ''heaven'', etc.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Would God'' I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!
{{right|2 Sam. xviii. 33.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I am not mad: I ''would to heaven'' I were!
For then ’tis like I should forget myself.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 4. 48.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To have a wish or desire; be willing.
{{smaller block|<poem>In a simile, as Eue
Was, whanne god ''wolde'' out of the wye y-drawe.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xix. 230.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The fomy brydel with the bit of gold
Governeth he, right as himself hath ''wold''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1209.}}}}
{{smaller block|All that falsen the kinges money or clippen it, also all that falsen or vse false measures, . . . wetyngly other than the lawe of the lord ''woll'', etc.
{{right|''J. Myrc'', Instructions for Parish Priests (E. E. T. S.), l. 714.}}}}
{{smaller block|They cryed to us to doe no more; all should be as we ''would''.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 191.}}}}

'''B.''' As an auxiliary, followed by an infinitive without ''to''. '''1.''' To wish, want, like, or agree (to do, etc.); to be (am, is, are, was, etc.) willing (to do, etc.): noting desire, preference, consent, or, negatively, refusal.
{{smaller block|<poem>But neuer man that place ne stede went
That sogerne ''wold'' ther for thyng any.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5804.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Quod Conscience, “thou flemed us from thee; Thou ''woldist'' not oure loore leere.”</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 76.}}}}
{{smaller block|That day that a man ''would'' have another’s landes or his goodes, that day he ''would'' have his life also if he could.
{{right|''Darrell Papers'', 1583 (H. Hall, Society in Elizabethan Age, [App. ii.).}}}}
{{smaller block|And ye ''will'' not come to me, that ye might have life.
{{right|John v. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|Oh, sir, the multitude, that seldom know any thing but their own opinions, speak that they ''would'' have.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Will'' you permit the orphan — nephew to whom you have been a father — to offer you a trifle [a ring]?
{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxx.}}}}
'''2.''' To be (am, is, are, etc.) determined (to do, etc.): said when one insists on or persists in being or doing something; hence, must, as a matter of will or pertinacity; do (emphatic auxiliary) from choice, wilfulness, determination, or persistence.
{{smaller block|<poem>Alas, the general might have pardon’d follies!
Soldiers ''will'' talk sometimes.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Fate’s such a shrewish thing,
She ''will'' be mistris.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, vi. 498.}}}}
{{smaller block|Some, not contented to haue them [Saxons] a people of German race, ''wil'' needs bring them from elsewhere.
{{right|''Verstegan'', Rest. of Decayed Intelligence (ed. 1628), p. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|There stand, if thou ''wilt'' stand.
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 551.}}}}
{{smaller block|If you ''will'' fling yourself under the wheels, Juggernaut will go over you, depend upon it.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Book of Snobs, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Cholera, scurvy, and fever, the wound that ''would'' not be heal’d.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Defence of Lucknow.}}}}

'''3.''' To make (it) a habit or practice (to do, etc.); be (am, is, are, etc.) accustomed (to do, etc.); do usually: noting frequent or customary action.

<poem>Joves halt it greet humblesse
And vertu eek, that thou ''wolt'' make
A nyght ful ofte thyn heed to ake.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 631.}}}}

{{smaller block|Whan he had souped at home in his house, he ''wolde'' call before hym all his seruauntes.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 29.}}}}

{{smaller block|I remember the hot summer Sunday afternoons, when the pavement ''would'' be red-hot, and the dust, and bits of straw, and scraps of paper, ''would'' blow fitfully about with every little puff of air.
{{right|''E. H. Yates'', Recollections and Experiences, I. vii.}}}}

'''4.''' To be (am, is, are, etc.) sure (to do, etc.); do undoubtedly, inevitably, or of necessity; ought or have (to do, etc.); must: used in incontrovertible or general statements, and often, especially in provincial use, forming a verb-phrase signifying no more than the simple verb: as, I’m thinking this ''will'' be (that is, this is) your daughter.

{{smaller block|I am aferd there ''wylle'' be sumthyng amys.
{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'' (ed. Halliwell), p. 395.}}}}

{{smaller block|Sixe comoun cubites, that ''wil'' be nyne foot long.
{{right|''Trevisa'', tr. of Higden’s Polychronicon (ed. Babington),}}
{{right|[II. 235.}}}}

{{smaller block|That ''will'' be unjust to man, ''will'' be sacrilegious to God.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xi.}}}}

{{smaller block|He was a considerate man, the deacon; . . . ye’''ll'' no hae forgotten him, Robin? {{right|''Scott'', Rob Roy, xxiii.}}}}

{{smaller block|A little difference, my dear. . . . There ''will'' be such in the best-regulated families. {{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xxvi.}}}}

{{smaller block|“Are you seeing any angels, Rob?” . . . “I’m not sure: . . . it is not easy to tell what ''will'' be an angel, and what ''will'' not. There ’s so much all blue up there.”
{{right|''Geo. MacDonald'', What’s Mine’s Mine, xix.}}}}

'''5.''' To be (am, is, are, etc.) ready or about (to do, etc.): said of one on the point of doing something not necessarily accomplished.

{{smaller block|As the queene hem saugh, she wiste well she was betraied, and ''wolde'' crye as she that was sore affraied, and thei seide that yef she spake eny worde she sholde a-non be slaine.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 463.}}}}

'''6.''' In future and conditional constructions, to be (am, is, are, etc.) (to do, etc.): in general noting in the first person a promise or determination, and in the second and third mere assertion of a future occurrence without reference to the will of the subject, other verb-phrases being compounded with the auxiliary ''shall.'' For a more detailed discrimination between ''will'' and ''shall'', see ''shall''<sup>1</sup>, B., 2.

<poem>And al the bettre sule ge speden,
If ge ''wilen'' gee with treweithe leden.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2304.}}}}

{{smaller block|Yef we ''willeth'' don his seruise . . . we sollen habbe tho mede wel griat ine heuene.
{{right|''Old Eng. Misc.'' (ed. Morris), p. 33.}}}}

<poem>At a knight than ''wol'' I first beginne.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 42.}}}}

<poem>''Wife.'' O, we shall have murder! you kill my heart.
''May.'' No, I ''will'' shed no blood.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 3.}}}}

<poem>Without their learning, how ''wilt'' thou with them,
Or they with thee, hold conversation meet?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 231.}}}}

<poem>Thou ''would’st'' have thought, so furious was their fire,
No force could tame them, and no toil could tire.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xv. 844.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was all to be done in the most delicate manner, and all ''would'' assist. Thackeray ''would'' lecture, so ''would'' W. H. Russell; Dickens ''would'' give a reading.
{{right|''E. H. Yates'', Recollections and Experiences, I. vii.}}}}
{{smaller|In such constructions ''will'' is sometimes found where precision would require ''shall.'' See ''shall''<sup>1</sup>, B., final note.}}
{{smaller block|I ''would'' have thought her spirit had been invincible against all assaults of affection.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 3. 119.}}}}
{{smaller block|If we contrast the present with so late a period as thirty years ago, we ''will'' perceive that there has been nothing short of a national awakening.
{{right|''W. Sharp'', D. G. Rossetti, p. 40.}}}}
{{smaller|[''Would'' is often used for ''will'' in order to avoid a dogmatic style or to soften blunt or harsh assertions, questions, etc.}}
{{smaller block|A pretty idle toy; ''would'' you take money for it?
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Would'' you say the Lord’s Prayer for me, old fellow?
{{right|''J. H. Ewing'', Six to Sixteen, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|In all its senses the auxiliary ''will'' may be used with an ellipsis of the following infinitive.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Bot I ''wyl'' to the chapel, for chaunce that may falle.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2132.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And Pandare wep as he to water ''wolde.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 115.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Pan.'' I heartily beseech you what must I do?
''Tronil.'' Even what thou ''wilt.''</poem>
{{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii. 36.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>First, then—A woman ''will'', or ''won’t''—depend on ’t;
If she will do ’t, she ''will''; and there ’s an end on ’t.</poem>
{{right|''A. Hill'', Zara, Epil.]}}}}

'''Will (you, he,''' etc.), '''nill (you, he,''' etc.). See ''nill''<sup>1</sup>.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
